items.title: Second Fractional Order Differential Constitutive Relations for Viscoelastic Materials of the Fractional Type with Piezoelectric Properties, Representing Rheological Models of Higher Complexity Levels
items.abstract: The author presents newly derived differential constitutive relations (equations) of the second fractional order for complex, higher-level rheological models of fractional-type viscoelastic materials with piezoelectric properties. These newly derived differential equations are of the second fractional order and incorporate Caputo differential operators of the first and second fractional orders. The lecturer outlines an approximate analytical methodology for solving these second-fractional-order differential equations, employing the Laplace transform, expansion into power series with respect to the complex Laplace parameter, and the properties of the convolution of three functions. This methodology yields approximate analytical solutions for the mew derived second-fractional-order differential constitutive equations governing these complex, higher-level rheological materials. These approximate analytical solutions simultaneously serve as integral constitutive relations, establishing the link between normal stresses and axial strains in these complex, higher-level rheological models of fractional-type viscoelastic materials with piezoelectric properties. The theoretical analytical results obtained pertain to complex fractional-type material models, specifically the second-level complexity Letherish-Faraday model for a fractional-type viscoelastic material with piezoelectric properties; The Jeffreys-Faraday model represents a second-level complexity rheological model for a fractional-type viscoelastic material with piezoelectric properties, while the Burgers-Faraday model represents a third-level complexity model of the same type. These three rheological models of higher complexity—in their classical linear forms—are already widely used; the author believes that the newly introduced fractional-type models (named by the author) will also see widespread application, initially in the validation of experimental research and subsequently in practical use. The lecturer also believes that these results open up new challenges regarding the development of software for calculating inverse Laplace transforms of complex Laplace-transformed expressions, thereby expanding the scope of artificial intelligence in areas where it is currently underdeveloped and limited.

items.title: Secondary School Teachers’ Interaction with Artificial Intelligence Systems: A Qualitative Investigation of Usability, Trust, and the Transformation of the Pedagogical Role
items.abstract: This research explores secondary education teachers" perceptions regarding the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into instructional practice. Through semi-structured interviews with a sample of ten (10) educators from diverse academic backgrounds, the study examines three core pillars: interaction and usability, issues of trust and ethics, and the transformation of professional identity. The findings reveal that using AI tools is a complex cognitive process requiring strategic prompt engineering. Despite the small sample size, participants consistently demonstrated a "cautious acceptance," acting as critical evaluators of machine-generated outputs to mitigate scientific inaccuracies and "hallucinations." In conclusion, the study highlights a shift in the teaching role from being a source of knowledge to an authority of critical mediation. It emphasizes the urgent need for professional development that fosters pedagogical agency and ethical action within the modern digital learning environment.

items.title: Semantic Communications and Edge Intelligence in 6G Wireless Networks: Task-Oriented Joint Source-Channel Coding and Latency Bounds
items.abstract: Abstract—As cellular architectures transition from 5G toward Sixth-Generation (6G) wireless networks, the classical Shannon-Nyquist paradigm of bit-level data transmission is rapidly approaching its theoretical physical channel capacity limits. Ultra-dense Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems, autonomous vehicular swarms, and extended reality (XR) telepresence demand terabit-per-second (Tbps) data rates, sub-millisecond latencies, and continuous real-time edge artificial intelligence (AI) inference over severely bandwidth-constrained wireless channels. Classical communications optimize bit error rates (BER), transmitting massive streams of uncompressed binary representations regardless of the underlying computational task. Semantic Communications and Task-Oriented Edge Intelligence establish a transformative paradigm shift: shifting the transmission objective from error-free bit reconstruction to the faithful transmission of actionable semantic meaning and task-relevant latent features. By uniting Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (Deep JSCC) with transformer-based feature extractors, semantic communication frameworks filter out redundant sensory data at the transmitter, communicating only task-critical representations to edge compute nodes. However, deploying semantic communications over stochastic wireless channels introduces acute foundational challenges: semantic noise induced by channel fading, joint training instability across non-differentiable wireless channels, and catastrophic performance degradation under out-of-distribution physical channel shifts. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of semantic communications for 6G edge intelligence. We formalize the rate-distortion-perception tradeoff under Weaver-Shannon semantic communication tiers, model continuous-time Deep JSCC over Rayleigh and Rician fading channels, and establish Lyapunov-guided end-to-end latency bounds for distributed edge inference. Furthermore, we construct an empirical software-defined radio (SDR) and GPU testbed evaluating multimodal perception and edge autonomous vehicle telemetry under severe signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) degradation. Our empirical findings demonstrate that Deep JSCC semantic transmission achieves a 78.4% reduction in required channel bandwidth while preserving 94.6% downstream edge classification accuracy under extreme channel noise (SNR = -6 dB), where classical JPEG/264 paired with LDPC coding completely collapses. Finally, we formulate open research directions in semantic knowledge base synchronization, neuro-symbolic semantic verification, and zero-trust semantic cybersecurity. Index Terms—Semantic Communications, 6G Wireless Networks, Edge Intelligence, Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (Deep JSCC), Task-Oriented Communications, Shannon-Weaver Levels, Physical Layer AI.

items.title: Service Recovery in Chatbot‐mediated Environments: Trust Dynamics and Customer Loyalty Intentions
items.abstract: Abstract Prior research has shown that customers’ perceptions of chatbots may be influenced by the situational context in which human–chatbot interactions take place. This research advances understanding of artificial intelligence (AI)‐enabled chatbot‐led service failure recovery (SFR) in the context of customer loyalty. Using a social constructivist philosophical perspective and an inductive approach, 52 in‐depth interviews were conducted to capture individuals’ perceptions of chatbot‐led interactions during a SFR process and how these perceptions impacted their trust in, and commitment to, brands. Utilizing commitment‐trust theory and trust transfer theory, we propose a framework that characterizes the relationships between a chatbot‐led SFR process and customer loyalty intentions. Based on the emergent data, customers’ evaluations of a service recovery journey led by chatbots can be grouped into four main outcomes: continued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand; continued trust in, and commitment to, brand; discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot; and discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand. Our findings extend current understanding of how consumers’ trust and commitment during chatbot‐led interactions during SFR evolve and highlight the dynamic relationship between consumers and the context of interactions. This study has theoretical and practical implications for developing and leveraging customers’ loyalty in AI‐enabled chatbot‐led SFR environments.

items.title: Sharenting as a Parenting Practice and the Recognition of the Child's Agency: A Transactional Analysis Perspective
items.abstract: This article examines sharenting practices among parents in relation to the recognition of the child's agency and the underlying relational mechanisms, interpreted through the lens of Educational Transactional Analysis (ETA). The empirical study employed a questionnaire-based survey of N = 420 parents of children aged 6-15 attending primary schools in Poznań, Poland. Statistical analyses (Welch's t test, Pearson's χ² test) revealed a digital privacy paradox: despite widespread endorsement of children's right to privacy, as many as 61.6% of parents of children aged 6–15 do not always ask their children for consent before publishing their image, or do not always respect their answers. This practice illustrates the discounting of the child's digital sovereignty from a paternalistic life position. Mothers were more likely than fathers to approach sharenting relationally, seeking digital strokes through the Child ego state. Higher self-assessed knowledge co-occurred with stronger concerns about artificial intelligence and with a propensity for corrective action (41.7% of parents had deleted previously posted photos of their child). The shift toward a position that recognizes the child as a subject occurs in response to adolescents' resistance or to parental self-reflection. The pedagogical implications point to the need for workshops on relational digital maturity and for promoting digital consent from the earliest years.

items.title: SimInter: Evidence-Grounded User Simulation with Interview-Based Profile Enrichment for Conversational Recommender Systems
items.abstract: Conversational Recommender Systems (CRSs) require reliable user simulators for cost-effective evaluation. LLM-based simulators have made realistic simulation possible but typically condition on profiles derived from explicit ratings, demographics, and static sources capturing surface preferences while omitting implicit behavioral characteristics such as decision-making style, aspect-level preferences, and domain expertise. We propose SimInter, a pipeline that elicits these attributes via synthetic interviews between two LLM agents, grounded in the user's statistical profile and historical conversational evidence. Before profile enrichment, an audit agent explicitly flags potential fabrication and stereotyping at the turn level. We instantiate and evaluate SimInter on movie recommendation. We simulate 300 ReDial users and, on a matched subset of 100 users, compare SimInter with a statistics-only baseline: SimInter significantly increases the diversity of expressed preference aspects (filtered aspect entropy: 1.619 vs. 0.859; paired d = 0.96, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). This gain persists when the simulator converses with two trained recommenders, KBRD and UniCRS, under two independent evaluation judges (+0.28 to +0.56 nats; all p < 0.001). Human evaluation finds 94.3% of enriched-attribute claims supported or partially supported, while human judgments agree with 95.2% of the auditor's binary filtering decisions on a stratified sample.

items.title: Simulation in the Development of Non-Technical Skills in Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Background: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) requires a coordinated and effective response, with non-technical skills (NTS) playing an important role in patient safety. Deficiencies in these skills may contribute to preventable clinical errors. Objectives: To map the scientific evidence on the contribution of simulation to the development of NTS among healthcare teams in the context of CPR. Methods: This scoping review followed JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting recommendations. MEDLINE, CINAHL, Nursing & Allied Health Collection: Comprehensive and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched via EBSCOhost up to 7 July 2026. Eligibility followed Population, Concept and Context criteria; two reviewers independently selected and charted the evidence. Results: The 27 included sources yielded three themes: simulation as a strategy for skill development; NTS in CPR; and complementary educational interventions. Communication was the most frequently reported NTS, alongside leadership, teamwork, situational awareness, and decision-making. Reported improvements varied across sources and skills, and some diminished or were only partially retained over time. Debriefing was addressed in 21 sources (77.8%). Evidence on complementary technologies remained preliminary, with some tools lacking formal evaluation or validation. Conclusions: The findings provide a descriptive map of heterogeneous evidence and suggest that simulation may support NTS development, particularly with structured debriefing. They do not establish effectiveness or effects on clinical outcomes. Robust quantitative and longitudinal studies using validated measures are needed to confirm observed trends and assess retention, transfer to practice, team performance, patient safety, and clinical outcomes.

items.title: SKILL-BASED TALENT MANAGEMENT AND AI-POWERED UPSKILLING AND RESKILLING: BRIDGING SKILL GAPS IN THE FUTURE WORKFORCE
items.abstract: Abstract: The workforce skill requirements across industries have been fundamentally redefined by the fast transition brought about by Industry 4.0 technologies, which include automation, big data analytics, artificial intelligence (AI), and cyber-physical systems. In order to address dynamic and technology-driven skill gaps, traditional role-based talent management approaches are becoming less and less effective. Continuous learning and ongoing education are emphasised as essential components in preparing employees to adapt to the shifting demands of the industry. This study looks at how upskilling and reskilling programs driven by AI may close skill gaps in the Industry 4.0 ecosystem to acquire the workforce ready for the future. Through the use of AI-enabled learning, ongoing competency development, and digital adaptability, the study creates a conceptual framework that connects skill-based talent management practices (an independent variable) with workforce agility and organisational success (dependent factors). In order to gather opinions from managers and workers in technology-intensive businesses, the study uses a quantitative research approach and standardised survey tools.AI integration in talent development procedures improves strategic workforce planning, decreases skill obsolescence, and promotes cultures of continuous learning.

items.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and $τ^2$-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.

items.title: Social Relationships in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Profound Shifts and New Challenges—An Integrative Literature Review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from a tool for information retrieval to a partner in conversation, advice, and emotional support. This integrative review examines whether that shift is reshaping friendship and other social bonds. Drawing on relationship science, human–machine communication research, surveys, experiments, longitudinal panels, randomized trials, and meta-analyses published through September 2026, including emerging evidence from Arab societies, the review develops the Responsiveness–Reciprocity Bridge Model to explain why conversational AI can relieve loneliness in the moment yet fail to build the relational capital that sustains people over time. A substantial minority of adolescents and young adults already turn to chatbots when they feel sad, anxious, or lonely, and short-term interactions with companion systems can reduce loneliness about as much as talking with another person, largely because users feel heard. These gains do not establish that synthetic ties can replace human friendship. Close relationships require mutual need, sacrifice, shared history, and practical solidarity that chatbots do not provide; in a randomized experiment, a human peer outperformed a highly supportive chatbot, and longitudinal and large-sample studies associate intensive, companionship-oriented use with greater loneliness and lower well-being. In Arab contexts, culturally aligned and human-guided digital tools show promise, but claims that AI is widely replacing traditional friends are not supported by comparable prevalence research. The central implication is balance: AI can widen access to support, but only if it is designed, governed, and used as a bridge to human relationships rather than as a substitute for them.

items.title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills
items.abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SkillTransferBench, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.

items.title: SpecCloak: Probing Harmful Code Generation through Engineering Specifications
items.abstract: The code generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs) can equally be misused to implement harmful functionality, underscoring the need to understand their safety behavior in response to programming requests. While request phrasing is known to influence refusal, it remains unclear whether the form in which coding task requirements are stated affects the refusal process for malicious code generation. We introduce PseudoSpec, a template that organizes functional requirements as engineering specifications, and investigate its effects through controlled comparisons, representation analysis, and activation interventions. Across five open-weight models, removing explicit risk keywords only partially reduces refusal, whereas specification prompting substantially lowers refusal even when these keywords are retained. This reduction accompanies consistent shifts toward code-output-related representations, and interventions along condition-difference directions alter refusal behavior. Output analysis further distinguishes code-related responses from generation degeneration. Building on these findings, we propose SpecCloak, a black-box red-teaming framework combining PseudoSpec with discriminator-guided optimization, achieving an average execution-verified attack success rate of 28.91\% across eight target models on RedCode-Gen. We also introduce SpecReveal, a defense prototype combining natural-language intent reconstruction with dual-view detection without target-model fine-tuning. It achieves a 96.88\% attack detection rate in a separate prompt-detection evaluation, with false positives assessed on benign programming and specification-style inputs. These results connect specification-induced response differences to practical security consequences and identify intent reconstruction as a complementary detection approach.

items.title: Spectral-MoE: Heterogeneous Per-Layer Expert Utilization in Dense-to-MoE Conversion
items.abstract: Large language models impose substantial memory demands and arithmetic costs during inference. Dense-to-mixture-of-experts (MoE) conversion is a model optimization technique that aims to reduce these arithmetic costs. Dense-to-MoE conversion partitions pretrained feed-forward network (FFN) neurons into experts and selects a subset for each token. Leading methods fall into two categories: analytic methods produce a converted model quickly using heuristics, while learning methods produce a model much more slowly by optimizing via gradients. Both approaches, however, fix the same active expert count, or "utilization," at every layer. We introduce Spectral-MoE, which learns to allocate a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers. Its name draws a metaphor between separating a dense FFN into experts and separating a light beam into its spectrum. Spectral-MoE consists of two distinct approaches: a static approach that uses a single per-layer scalar which is shared across tokens, and a dynamic approach which emits a per-token schedule. We demonstrate that both allocators improve performance over uniform on both the analytic-based and learning-based SOTA dense-to-MoE methods. At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation reduces WikiText-2 perplexity relative to uniform by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on the learned base for Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. The corresponding reductions on the analytic base are 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points. On the learned base, dynamic allocation improves six-task mean accuracy over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points across the three models at FFN utilizations of 12.5%, 25%, and 50%, respectively. These results establish per-layer expert utilization as a novel optimization axis in dense-to-MoE conversion.

items.title: Stable Token-level Scheduling for Serverless LLM Inference
items.abstract: Serverless inference is emerging as an efficient deployment model for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its ability to elastically scale resources, improve GPU utilization through resource sharing, and reduce infrastructure costs. However, existing approaches primarily optimize time to first token (TTFT) while overlooking inter-token latency (ITL), a key determinant of user experience during response generation. We observe that LLM inference comprises a computation-intensive prefill stage and a bandwidth-bound decode stage, where admitting new requests can disrupt ongoing decoding and increase latency. To address this, we propose Token Window Pacing (TWP), a closed-loop scheduling framework that leverages runtime feedback from ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to regulate request admission at the token level instead of the batch level. TWP dynamically adjusts a selfregulating token window and incorporates chunk-based prefill to minimize interference from incoming requests. Experiments on realistic serverless workloads show that TWP delivers stable TTFT, significantly reduces latency spikes, lowers P99 tail latency, minimizes ITL variation, and improves throughput by up to 45% over ServerlessLLM and 58% over conventional schedulers. These results demonstrate that feedback-driven tokenlevel scheduling enables stable, high-throughput serverless LLM inference without modifying the underlying model.

items.title: Structural Analysis of Mat Foundations in Soft Soil of Basra City, Iraq
items.abstract: Purpose: This study aims to evaluate suitable foundation systems for a three-story building constructed on soft soil in the centre of Basra City, Iraq. The study assesses the structural response, bearing capacity, punching shear, and settlement behaviour of different foundation types to identify an appropriate and practical foundation solution. Design/Methodology/Approach: The structural analysis of the three-story building was performed using STAAD.Pro to determine the reactions at the building supports. Subsequently, SAFE was used to model and analyse different foundation systems, including isolated footings, strip footings, and mat foundations with and without beams. The foundation systems were evaluated based on punching shear and settlement criteria. Research Limitation: The study focuses on a three-story building and the specific soft-soil conditions of central Basra; therefore, the findings may not be directly applicable to buildings with significantly different heights or soil conditions. Findings: The results indicated that all investigated foundation systems satisfied the punching shear requirements. However, most isolated footings exceeded the permissible settlement limit of 25.4 mm. Although the strip footing remained within the allowable settlement limit, its application was considered impractical because of its limited economic feasibility and construction difficulties. The mat foundation modelled as a flat slab achieved a maximum settlement of 14 mm, while the mat foundation with beams recorded a maximum settlement of 19.8 mm. Practical Implication: The results indicate that mat foundations are suitable for low-rise buildings on soft soil. The mat foundation with beams provides a more economical alternative to the flat-slab mat foundation. Social Implication: Selecting an appropriate foundation system can improve building safety, reduce construction risks, and contribute to more reliable and sustainable urban development in areas characterised by soft soil. Originality/Value: This study compares foundation alternatives for low-rise buildings on soft soil in Basra, offering practical guidance for selecting safe and economically feasible foundation systems.

items.title: Student perceptions of generative AI in accounting education: A thematic analysis
items.abstract: Generative AI has outpaced pedagogical and ethical guidance in accounting classrooms, leaving students and educators uncertain whether it supports or undermines the discipline's dual emphasis on procedural accuracy and professional judgment. To address this problem, this study examines how 92 business undergraduates perceive generative AI tools, notably ChatGPT, in accounting education, drawing on in-class, handwritten survey responses. Findings show that students view AI as a useful yet uncertain resource: valuing its speed, accessibility, and support while raising concerns over cheating, fairness, unclear institutional policies, and overreliance. Four interconnected themes emerged: Practical Affordances and Engagement, Ethical Tensions and Integrity, Curricular and Institutional Context, and Reflective Learning and Active Engagement. These results suggest student perceptions are shaped less by technology alone than by the pedagogical and ethical conditions of its introduction. Theoretically, the study identifies an augmentation–formation paradox specific to disciplines that combine codifiable procedure with professional judgment, which is advanced tentatively as extending the boundary conditions of paradox theory in education, a proposition that requires further empirical testing. Thematic analysis using a hybrid inductive–deductive coding strategy served as the primary analytic approach, supported by supplementary lexical analyses. The study contributes to management and accounting education by demonstrating that responsible AI integration requires clear guidance, reflective learning, and explicit alignment among AI use, assessment design, and academic integrity.

items.title: SUSHILA: Scalable Upstream Synthesis for Hybrid Inference in Large-model Acceleration
items.abstract: This paper starts from existing open-source weights, stacks new inference research on top of the optimization techniques already in use, and produces faster inference of the same model—without changing a single weight. Sushila.cpp is a free, local inference engine built on top of llama.cpp, the open-source engine behind Ollama, with SGLang on NVIDIA servers. Large language models are slow and expensive to run mainly because every generated token reads the model’s weights (for mixture-of-experts models, its active experts) from memory again. SUSHILA (Scalable Upstream Synthesis for Hybrid Inference in Large-model Acceleration) tests the published speed-up methods on each model once, right after its release, keeps those that make it faster at unchanged quality, and adds methods of our own. One of them, a landscape precomputed once per model, previews every next-token score cheaply, then computes only the best candidates exactly, reading 13–15% of the output layer with ≥99.75% agreement on the top token (7–70B models). Over eight GPU chat and coding models, Sushila.cpp achieves a geometric-mean speedup of 2.35× over Ollama (up to 4.05× on Llama-3.3-70B, on 160 benchmark prompts it never saw, with GSM8K accuracy unchanged within its error bars), measured on an NVIDIA A100 with Sushila.cpp’s SGLang serving path. Most of this gain comes from existing methods; our precomputed draft heads add 1–11% where a good head was already published and are most of the gain where none was: 3.64× on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B and 3.56× on Kimi-Dev-72B. Speed tests were done on one NVIDIA A100 80GB for chat and coding models (media mostly on one RTX 4090; engine-level tests also on CPUs), one user at a time; results may vary on other computers. Every result has its scripts and raw outputs in our public repository, and each chat and coding comparison reruns with one command.

items.title: System analysis approaches for the development of advanced architectures
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has established a new technological and organizational landscape across all industries, yet the process of creating AI architecture remains disjointed, intuitive, and domain-oriented. The proposed study introduces a System-Analytical Framework of Artificial Intelligence Architecture Design (SA-AI Framework), a collection of principles from systems analysis and multi-criteria decision-making intended to harmonize architectural design processes across heterogeneous AI domains. The paper is based on twenty-five current studies in explainable AI, neural-symbolic architectures, human-centered robotics, agentic systems, and domain-specific applications, such as healthcare, finance, energy, and education, that inform a comparative synthesis of architectural design principles. A Research Design Science Research (DSR) approach is used to model and test the SA-AI Framework conceptually across four stages: requirements analysis, identification of architectural alternatives, multi-criteria evaluation, and model validation. Results show that the framework offers a systematic, defensible method for constructing AI architectures, enabling greater exposure, flexibility, and decision-making effectiveness. It has cohesively unified the different models of AI, including the agentic AI, Explainable AI (XAI), Human-Centered AI (HCAI), and safety-driven architectures, providing both theory and practice to AI engineering and policy design. This paper concludes that system analysis helps design AI systems that integrate both technical and socio-technical systems to enhance the governance, reliability, and sustainability of intelligent architecture in the next generation.

items.title: Teach Me After You Learn It: Lookahead Self-Distillation for RLVR
items.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a popular training paradigm for LLMs, providing dense, token-level supervision by aligning a model's own distribution with the distribution induced by privileged information. However, existing OPSD methods derive supervision solely from privileged information of the same instance, leaving inter-instance supervision largely unexplored. We propose Lookahead Self-Distillation (LEAD), which introduces inter-instance distillation by allowing the teacher to first learn from other on-policy rollouts before teaching the student. LEAD constructs lookahead teachers through virtual RL updates on disjoint subsets of on-policy rollouts, and uses each teacher to provide cross-group token-level supervision for the other subset. To reconcile the complementary yet potentially conflicting signals from OPSD and RLVR, we introduce harmonious modulation, which adaptively modulates the GRPO advantage based on the agreement between the two signals. Extensive experiments on scientific reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks show that LEAD achieves the best in-domain average performance across model scales while maintaining out-of-domain generalization comparable to GRPO.

items.title: Teacher Factors Influencing Elementary Students’ Mathematics Learning Motivation: a PRISMA 2020 Systematic Review
items.abstract: Elementary students’ mathematics learning motivation declines systematically across early schooling and predicts subsequent academic achievement, yet no prior systematic review has integrated the instructional, relational, emotional, and epistemological dimensions of teacher influence within a single framework. This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching Scopus on 30 March 2025 using a PEO-based Boolean strategy; 531 unique records were screened, yielding 16 included studies whose methodological quality was appraised using MMAT 2018 and synthesized through thematic narrative synthesis. Findings indicate that autonomy-supportive instruction and formative assessment enhance intrinsic motivation, positive teacher-student relationships correlate with motivation while conflict and dependency undermine it, teacher mindfulness programs yield modest but causally demonstrated effects, and inquiry-oriented epistemological beliefs indirectly raise student motivation through teacher efficacy. An integrated four-channel model of teacher influence is proposed, providing an evidence base for teacher professional development programs that simultaneously target instructional, relational, emotional, and epistemological competencies, particularly relevant to Indonesia’s Kurikulum Merdeka reform. items.title: Teacher-Facing Generative AI and Workplace Mental Health in Higher Education: Perceived Demands and Resources
items.abstract: To read the full-text Open Access article and download the PDFs, please visit our Issue portal at Paradigm (Walter de Gruyter): https://reference-global.com/article/10.56508/mhgcj.v9i1.374 Introduction: Workplace mental health promotion in higher education requires attention to how digital technologies reshape teaching demands and resources. Purpose: To identify perceived demands and resources surrounding teacher-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) and interpret their implications for teachers’ mental health promotion. Methodology: An exploratory mixed-methods study combined a survey of 150 participants (56 English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers and 94 students/student-tutors) with 12 teacher interviews at two Ukrainian universities in January-February 2026. Descriptive statistics and four exploratory Fisher exact tests with Holm adjustment were integrated with thematic analysis of 30 selected translated interview extracts. Job Demands-Resources and self-determination theories informed a post-hoc interpretation. Results: Among teachers, 53.6% rated an AI platform for EFL teachers (Twee) very useful for preparation-time saving and 57.1% for task variety. Across the mixed sample, access (27.3%), quality assurance (22.0%), curriculum alignment (20.0%), and training/time (20.0%) were the leading constraints. Interview extracts linked anticipated workload relief to individual student support, while highlighting learning demands and the importance of professional judgment, empathy, and mentoring. Conclusions: These perceptions identify work-design issues relevant to mental health promotion during AI implementation. Participatory decisions, protected learning and recovery time, and accessible psychosocial support are priorities for institutional consideration

items.title: TEACHERS' DECISION-MAKING IN ADAPTING AI-GENERATED ACADEMIC TEXTS FOR TASK-BASED LANGUAGE TEACHING (TBLT) IN UZBEKISTAN
items.abstract: This thesis analyzes teachers’ pedagogical decision-making in selecting and adapting artificial intelligence-generated academic texts for Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT) in the context of teaching English as a foreign language (EFL) in Uzbekistan. The study considers texts generated by generative AI tools not as ready-to-use teaching materials, but as resources that require linguistic, content-related, and methodological evaluation and adaptation by teachers to suit specific learning tasks. Particular attention is paid to teachers’ decisions based on lexical and grammatical complexity, content accuracy and reliability, students’ language proficiency, the characteristics of academic discourse, the communicative purpose of the task, and relevance to the local educational context. The study also systematizes adaptation strategies such as simplifying and shortening texts, replacing lexical items, contextualizing content, and transforming texts into TBLT tasks. The analysis demonstrates that artificial intelligence does not automatically guarantee pedagogically appropriate materials and that the quality of the final learning materials depends on teachers’ professional judgment, linguistic competence, and methodological decisions.

items.title: Teaching English as a Second Language in an Evolving Digital Landscape
items.abstract: Intensive English Programs have undergone major changes in how technology supports language education and research. At the University of Pittsburgh&s;s English Language Institute, early efforts centered on custom-built software that supported both classroom instruction and research, culminating in projects such as the PELIC corpus. Over time, however, there has been an industry-wide shift toward off-the-shelf platforms emphasizing usability and integration, often at the cost of research adaptability. Throughout these shifts, work in linguistics, applied linguistics, and related fields (such as second language studies, corpus linguistics, and psycholinguistics) have remained a key influence, and these areas have been strongly influenced by the scholarship of Alan Juffs. Looking ahead, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as large language models offer personalized learning opportunities but also pose risks. They challenge assumptions about the assessment of linguistic proficiency and complicate future research by undermining the provenance of learner-provided text. The PELIC corpus, completed under Juffs’ leadership just before the rise of GenAI, serves as a gift to future research, capturing robust learner data from the “pre-AI” era.

items.title: Teaching Generation Z: The Pedagogical Innovation Pentagon For Hybrid Introductory Marketing Education
items.abstract: This study examines how pedagogical innovation can support Generation Z students in post-COVID marketing education, where hybrid learning and artificial intelligence are reshaping course design. It introduces the Pedagogical Innovation Pentagon, an evidence-informed model organized around five interrelated dimensions: hybridization, digitalization, artificial intelligence, responsibility, and harmonization. The model was developed and evaluated through a mixed-methods exploratory study conducted with first-year students enrolled in a bilingual introductory marketing course within a multi-campus business program. The model was implemented through an Instructional Capsule, a structured learning environment combining bilingual content development, guided activities, feedback mechanisms, sustainability-focused case studies, and shared assessment practices across campuses. Student self-reports and course analytics were used to explore how this instructional approach supported engagement, clarity, feedback, ethical awareness, and coherence in students’ learning experiences. Findings suggest that effective innovation in marketing education depends less on technological sophistication than on the meaningful integration of digital tools within a human-centered and ethically intentional learning environment. The study contributes to marketing education by offering a transferable approach for integrating digital transformation, AI, and responsible pedagogy into course design and continuous improvement.

items.title: TEACHING PRACTICES OF GRADE 8 SCIENCE TEACHERS EMBEDDED WITH AI-DRIVEN ADAPTIVE LEARNING SYSTEM IN SCIENCE INSTRUCTION
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to personalize science instruction, yet evidence regarding teachers’ AI-supported practices and learners’ cognitive engagement remains limited. This study examined Grade 8 Science teachers’ practices embedded with AI-driven adaptive learning systems at Bongabon National High School, Nueva Ecija, during school year 2026–2027. Specifically, it described teachers’ profiles and practices across planning and preparation, classroom environment, instruction, and professional responsibilities, and investigated relationships and differences in respondents’ perceptions. A descriptive survey design with quasi-experimental designation, involved six Grade 8 Science teachers and 499 students. Teacher respondents were covered through complete enumeration, while student respondents were selected through simple random sampling. Questionnaires provided data analyzed using frequencies, percentages, weighted means, t-tests, and Spearman’s rho. Findings indicated that AI-embedded teaching practices were “Always Practiced,” with an overall grand weighted mean of 3.60. Classroom environment obtained the highest combined domain mean (3.64), followed by instruction (3.62), planning and preparation (3.59), and professional responsibilities (3.55). Teachers’ educational attainment showed significant negative relationships with planning and preparation (rho = −0.892) and classroom environment (rho = −0.874), whereas other profile variables showed no significant relationships. Teachers’ and learners’ perceptions did not differ significantly across domains. The study concluded that AI-supported teaching practices were consistently reported and recommended targeted professional development and activities to strengthen comparatively less-practiced areas. These findings may guide context-responsive integration of adaptive learning tools in junior high school Science instruction while supporting reflective teaching practice and student engagement. This supports responsible implementation.

items.title: Teaming or friction? Human–AI collaboration with a Multimodal Digital Intelligent Assistant in assembly manufacturing
items.abstract: The transition toward Industry 5.0 promotes human-centred production systems in which digital technologies augment human capabilities rather than replace them. Within this paradigm, Digital Intelligent Assistants have emerged as promising tools to support operators during complex industrial tasks. Moreover, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), including Large Language Models and Vision Language Models, enables the development of such systems by combining natural language interaction with visual perception. This exploratory mixed-methods pilot study investigates the impact of a multimodal Digital Intelligent Assistant (M-DIA) designed to support operators during a manual assembly process. A controlled laboratory experiment involving 60 participants compared four conditions: multimodal interaction (voice and camera), voice-only interaction, camera-only interaction, and a manual baseline. The analysis considered process performance, perceived cognitive workload, usability and user experience, and operator behaviour. The results show that M-DIA improves assembly quality by reducing product errors compared with the manual condition, although no reduction in total process time is observed due to interaction-related delays. From a human perspective, the assistant reduces perceived cognitive workload, while higher frustration levels emerge in configurations involving voice interaction. Usability and user experience evaluations are overall positive across all experimental conditions. Behavioural observations further indicate that operators maintain an active supervisory role, critically assessing system outputs and avoiding systematic overreliance on the assistant. These findings provide preliminary empirical evidence on the role of GenAI-based multimodal assistants in human-centred manufacturing and highlight key design implications for their industrial deployment.

items.title: Technology-enhanced and AI-supported instruction: a meta-analysis of student learning outcomes with implications for writing development
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has introduced new paradigms for teaching, learning, and assessment, especially in the development of students’ writing performance. This meta-analysis examines the effectiveness of blended, technology-enhanced, and AI-supported instructional interventions on student learning outcomes. Eleven studies representing 477 participants across primary, secondary, and higher-education settings were synthesized. The included studies represented heterogeneous educational contexts and assessed outcomes such as academic achievement, literacy, vocabulary and language learning, digital literacy, and motivation. Accordingly, the pooled effect represents an overall effect on student learning outcomes rather than a writing-proficiency-specific effect. Studies were identified through ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar and represented 477 participants across elementary, secondary, and higher-education settings and diverse disciplinary contexts. The results revealed a large and statistically significant pooled effect size [Hedges’ g = 0.89, 95% CI (0.76, 1.10)], showing that students who participated in technology-enhanced instructional interventions outperformed those receiving traditional instruction. Exploratory moderator analyses showed differences according to educational level, intervention duration, and technology type, with primary and secondary students, medium-length interventions (4–8 weeks), and interactive tools showing the strongest effects. The findings show the potential of thoughtfully integrated digital and AI-supported tools to enhance teaching and learning.

items.abstract: In this interview with Qiu Zeqi, professor at Peking University and internationally recognized intellectual, we explore aspects related to his academic trajectory and inquire about the complex relationship between technology and society, both in general and specifically in China. The focus of the questions lies within the field of Science and Technology Studies (STS) in China, addressing historical elements that shaped the foundations of Chinese society, as well as contemporary themes, challenges and their possible developments. Additionally, Professor Qiu offers thought-provoking reflections on Brazil-China relations across various sectors. The overarching objective is to understand these elements and their interplay with technology through an exploratory qualitative interview, drawing on the author’s articles and works. Thus, the interview contributes to a deeper comprehension of key themes in the STS field, recent processes of sociotechnical transformation in China, future perspectives associated with the evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, and reflections for Brazil and Latin America. items.title: textGrain watermarking is harder to detect: can sum-tests still do it optimally?
items.abstract: Watermarking embeds an imperceptible signal in text from large language models that is statistically detectable with a secret key. The recent textGrain watermark (Li et. al. (2026b)) calibrates this signal against the model's sampling entropy through an explicit entropy budget, combining the stochasticity of Red-Green and the unbiasedness of Gumbel-max watermarks, and its accompanying report proposes a detector that sums pivotal statistics. We study when, and how efficiently, textGrain can be detected after human edits, modeled as a sparse mixture in which a fraction $\varepsilon_n\asymp n^{-p}$ of positions retain the watermark and token uncertainty decays as $n^{-q}$. First, entropy calibration comes at a cost: the minimax detection boundary of textGrain is $p+q=1/2$, so its detectable region is strictly smaller than that of Gumbel-max and maximal-coupling watermarks, whose boundary is $2p+q=1$. This cost stems from textGrain's construction rather than from entropy calibration itself: an unbiased scheme with the same entropy loss remains detectable where textGrain is not. Second, perhaps surprisingly, this loss makes the sum detector optimal at the boundary when the number of transport columns is fixed, unlike for Gumbel-max. When the number of columns grows and the entropy budget does not vanish, the detectable region expands while that of the sum detector does not. Third, for a fixed edit fraction, we characterize the optimal exponential rate of type II error decay and show that the sum detector falls strictly short of it at every fixed alternative. Finally, we propose a weighted multiscale binomial scan, valid in finite samples and needing no knowledge of the next-token distributions, entropy budget, or edit fraction; it attains every detection boundary above and the optimal exponent.

items.title: TextualRL: Textual Reinforcement Learning for Context Management
items.abstract: LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. We introduce TextualRL, a gradient-free reinforcement learning framework that treats a group of rollouts from the same task under the same context, rather than an isolated trajectory, as the unit of policy critique. Groupwise Policy Critique contrasts successful and failed rollouts within a task; when outcomes are uniform, it draws on cross-task evidence to identify behaviors worth preserving or formulate repair hypotheses. Cross-Group Policy Update reviews the resulting proposals against evidence pooled across groups, including observations that yield no proposed edit, to refine their content and applicability. Reviewed proposals form a bounded textual patch, with adoption of the candidate context determined by held-out validation rewards. Together, these components establish a reward-driven policy optimization loop in which multiple attempts jointly inform reusable context updates. We evaluate TextualRL with five target agents on six benchmarks. Averaged over the six benchmarks, TextualRL improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 and 15.3 percentage points for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.8-27B, respectively.

items.title: The AI dilemma in L2 writing: Is AI literacy associated with willingness to write through self-efficacy, anxiety, or both? A serial mediation investigation
items.abstract: This study investigates the psychological mechanisms through which artificial intelligence (AI) literacy relates to L2 learners’ willingness to write (WTW). It proposes a serial mediation model wherein L2 writing self-efficacy (WSE) and L2 writing anxiety (WA) sequentially mediate this relationship. Grounded in social cognitive theory and control-value theory, the research employed a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design with 303 Chinese EFL learners. Quantitative results from structural equation modeling indicate that: (1) L2 WSE fully mediates the relationship between AI literacy and L2 WTW; (2) AI literacy is indirectly linked to L2 WTW through a sequential pathway: by first positively predicting L2 WSE, which in turn negatively predicts L2 WA; and (3) the direct effects of AI literacy on L2 WA and L2 WTW are non-significant. To explain these quantitative pathways, qualitative interviews with 16 participants further elucidated how AI tool usage corresponds to higher L2 WSE through strategic partnership, reduced startup burden, and task scaffolding support. Furthermore, the qualitative narratives revealed that while AI usage can initially be associated with anxiety (e.g., fear of exposure, tool-related frustration), the heightened L2 WSE linked to AI literacy effectively serves as a protective factor against these affective barriers. The study concludes that AI literacy positively correlates with L2 WTW through a fully indirect mechanism, in which heightened L2 WSE serves as a vital prerequisite for lowering L2 WA. These findings contribute to theory by integrating two major psychological frameworks and offer practical implications for leveraging AI to cultivate more willing L2 writers.

items.title: The Augmented Physician
items.abstract: In 2016, a leading AI researcher predicted that machine learning would render radiologists obsolete within five years. A decade later, the opposite has happened. Radiology is among the most competitive specialties in medicine, and artificial intelligence has become a tool that makes physicians faster, more accurate, and more capable rather than a force that replaces them. This chapter traces that shift across radiology, pathology, ophthalmology, cardiology, and stroke and diabetic eye care, where AI now detects disease, triages urgent cases, and extends screening to populations that were previously underserved. The recurring lesson is that augmentation, not automation, defines AI’s clinical value, and that its safe and effective use depends on physicians who understand both its capabilities and its limits. By establishing this framing, the chapter sets up the practical questions the rest of the book addresses: how to evaluate AI tools, integrate them into clinical workflows, navigate the ethical challenges they raise, and redefine physician expertise for a new era of medicine.

items.title: The Bosadi-Salutogenic framework: culturally embedded identity as a personal resource for work engagement among Black South African women in middle management
items.abstract: The dominance of Euro-American frameworks in industrial and organizational psychology has rendered culturally embedded work experiences largely invisible. While foundational models such as the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework elegantly illuminate universal engagement mechanisms across diverse contexts, occupational health literature has traditionally paid less attention to how intersecting racialized and gendered identities shape occupational well-being in postcolonial settings. This conceptual paper addresses this contextual gap by examining the organizational position of Black women in South African middle management, a group navigating unique structural tensions rooted in historical exclusion and contemporary marginalization. Responding to calls for disciplinary decolonization, I propose an integrated Afrocentric framework that brings Bosadi theorization into conversation with salutogenic principles. Specifically, I argue that Bosadi identity functions are not merely as a demographic marker but as a culturally embedded personal resource that shapes how job demands are interpreted, managed, and made meaningful. By positioning identity as an analytic resource rather than a contextual variable, the framework extends the JD-R model’s explanatory power to account for culturally specific modes of resilience and meaning-making. The paper concludes by outlining theoretical contributions to organizational psychology and offering directions for empirical research, including methodological considerations for studying culturally situated work experiences. This work aims to support the development of organizational practices that are genuinely responsive to the lived realities of historically marginalized women.

items.title: The Development of Micro Game-Based Learning Model on Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment
items.abstract: This study aimed to synthesize, develop, and evaluate the Micro Game-Based Learning Model on Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment. The study integrated Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and Metaverse technologies to create a learning environment that provides short learning units, interactive game-based activities, and simulated communication situations. The research objectives were to (1) synthesize the learning process, (2) develop the learning model, and (3) evaluate the learning model. The evaluation panel consisted of three experts from various academic institutions. The experts were selected based on their experience at least 3 years in education, instructional design and development, particularly in teaching English for communication. The research instruments consisted of the learning model, learning platform, and an expert evaluation questionnaire based on a 5-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics according to the research objectives. The findings indicated that the appropriateness of the developed learning model was evaluated at a highest level (Mean = 4.93, SD = 0.24). The findings suggest that integrating Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and an Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment provides a feasible approach for developing technology-supported English communication learning.

This study improves the relevant theoretical system, and also provides practical reference for teacher training, intelligent teaching platform optimization and evaluation reform. items.title: The Eames chair and the culture industry: A critical analysis of the democratization of modern design.
items.abstract: This article critically examined the Eames DSS Stacking chair (1950) as a paradigmatic case of the tensions between the democratization of modern design and the logics of industrial capitalism. The central problem lay in the contradiction between its emancipatory promise — making functional and aesthetic design accessible to the masses — and its entanglement in the standardization, pseudo-individualization, and commodification dynamics characteristic of the Culture Industry. Using a qualitative case-study approach, the research applied a theoretical triangulation combining Adorno and Horkheimer’s theory, Benjamin’s reflections on technical reproducibility, and Llovet’s semiotics of value as reinterpreted by Anderson and Girod. The analysis revealed that, while the chair achieved a massive distribution exceeding 20 million units and represented a significant ergonomic breakthrough, it simultaneously sacrificed artisanal singularity, subordinated use-value to capitalist exchange-value, and reproduced ideological mechanisms of cultural control. The research further showed that the chair’s contemporary reception in institutions such as MoMA demonstrates capitalism’s capacity to absorb and recycle its own critiques, transforming objects with a democratizing vocation into icons of cultural distinction. The study concludes that any genuinely democratizing design proposal must confront these structural contradictions rather than merely celebrating technical efficiency or superficial accessibility.

items.title: The Future of Fashion
items.abstract: This chapter examines how circular economy (CE) imaginaries are articulated and stabilised within the fashion industry. Drawing on the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, it analyses the Global Fashion Summit 2025 as a field-configuring event where competing visions of circular transition are publicly performed. Based on participant observation, session recordings, and field notes, the study identifies five distinct CE imaginaries. The findings show that these imaginaries stabilise unevenly through discourses, representations, institutions, and identities, shaping how circularity becomes actionable. The chapter contributes to fashion business and management research by demonstrating that CE transition is not governed by a single coherent pathway, but constructed through multiple co-existing visions that prioritise different problems, solutions, and actors.

items.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Personalized Learning on Korean Language Performance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming foreign language learning from traditional knowledge transmission into a data-driven adaptive learning process. Grounded in Personalized Learning Theory and technology-enhanced learning (TEL), this study examines the impact of AI application on Korean language learning performance (KAP) from the perspective of technological mediation and further explores the mediating role of intelligent recommendation systems (IRSs). Using questionnaire and academic performance data from 850 undergraduate students majoring in the Korean language, the study employs multiple regression and mediation analysis to test the proposed relationships. The results indicate that AI application significantly improves KAP (β = 4.684, p < 0.01) and exerts a significant partial mediating effect through IRSs. Specifically, AI application significantly increases the utilization of IRSs (β = 3.127, p < 0.01), while IRSs further enhance learning performance (β = 2.827, p < 0.01). Marginal effect analysis further reveals that the positive effect of AI is strongest at moderate usage levels, whereas excessive AI use leads to diminishing marginal returns. The findings demonstrate that AI not only directly improves learning outcomes through real-time feedback, speech recognition, and personalized learning support, but also promotes resource allocation optimization and dynamic learning path adjustment through AI-driven adaptive learning mechanisms. This study extends the mechanism-oriented explanation of AI-assisted language learning within the context of Korean language education and provides theoretical and practical implications for the development of intelligent and personalized Korean language learning platforms in higher education.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ASSISTED LEARNING ON EFL LEARNERS' SPEAKING PROFICIENCY: EVIDENCE FROM UZBEK UNIVERSITY STUDENTS
items.abstract: Abstract. The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for improving English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, particularly in the development of speaking proficiency. AI-powered chatbots, speech recognition systems, conversational agents, and generative AI applications enable learners to practise English, receive immediate feedback, and engage in interactive communication beyond the traditional classroom. This article examines the potential impact of AI-assisted learning on EFL learners’ speaking proficiency, with particular attention to the educational context of Uzbek universities. It explores the ways in which AI-based tools may support speaking fluency, pronunciation, grammatical accuracy, vocabulary development, learner confidence, and willingness to communicate. Drawing on existing research and pedagogical perspectives, the article discusses the opportunities and limitations of integrating AI into higher education. Particular attention is given to speaking anxiety, unequal access to digital resources, feedback reliability, learner autonomy, and the importance of teacher guidance. The analysis suggests that AI can serve as a valuable supplementary resource when integrated into structured pedagogical activities. However, its effectiveness depends on learners’ engagement, instructional design, and the combination of technological practice with authentic human interaction. Further empirical research involving Uzbek university students is necessary to establish the extent and long-term effects of AI-assisted speaking instruction. Keywords: artificial intelligence, EFL learners, speaking proficiency, AI-assisted learning, university students, conversational AI, language anxiety, Uzbekistan, digital education.

items.title: The Relationship Between Job Satisfaction and Work Stress Among Teachers
items.abstract: Work stress is a common occupational health problem among teachers and may affect psychological well-being and the quality of teaching. One factor suspected to be associated with work stress is job satisfaction. This study aimed to analyze the relationship between job satisfaction and work stress among teachers at SMP Negeri 14 and SMP Negeri 18, South Tangerang City. This study employed a quantitative design with a cross-sectional approach. The study population consisted of 96 active teachers from both schools, with 93 teachers meeting the study criteria and participating through total sampling. Data were collected using a respondent characteristics questionnaire, the Job Satisfaction Survey (JSS) to measure job satisfaction, and the Job Stress Scale to measure work stress. Data analysis included univariate and bivariate analyses using the Chi-Square test at a 95% significance level. The results showed that 39.8% of respondents had low job satisfaction, 25.8% were categorized as ambivalent, and 34.4% had high job satisfaction. Most respondents (65.6%) experienced low work stress, while 34.4% experienced high work stress. Bivariate analysis revealed a significant relationship between job satisfaction and work stress (p < 0.001; OR = 8.27; 95% CI: 3.06–22.39), indicating that teachers with low job satisfaction had a higher risk of experiencing work stress than those with high job satisfaction. In addition, age, gender, and teaching workload were significantly associated with work stress. The study concludes that improving job satisfaction through improvements in the work environment, reward systems, organizational communication, and workload management is an important strategy for reducing work stress and enhancing teachers’ well-being.

items.title: The Responsibility Gap in Explainable AI
items.abstract: This paper critically examines the persistent responsibility gap in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), arguing that current approaches fail to adequately bridge it. While XAI is often promoted as a remedy for the opacity of AI systems—the so-called “black box problem”—and as a way to enable human accountability in both high- and low-stakes AI applications, I contend that these hopes are premature. The paper distinguishes between legal and moral responsibility, arguing that regulation alone cannot address the full spectrum of responsibility gaps, especially in everyday, low-stakes scenarios. Then, I argue that XAI needs to tackle two separate but interconnected problems in its attempt to bridge the responsibility gap: an epistemological problem concerning the nature of XAI explanations, and a moral attribution problem regarding the distribution of blame and praise in situations where AI is involved in decision-making. Through detailed discussion of XAI methods and their limitations, I demonstrate that existing techniques often provide only post-hoc, technically focused explanations, which are insufficient for grounding moral responsibility. The paper concludes that without fundamental advances in both the design of explanations and our practices of responsibility attribution, the responsibility gap in AI will remain an unresolved and pressing issue for the field.

items.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN LEARNING MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
items.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning management systems (LMS) in higher education. It analyses how AI can support personalized learning, automated assessment, intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, and teachers’ instructional work. A conceptual approach is used to synthesize relevant literature and identify practical integration principles. The analysis indicates that AI-enabled LMS functions may improve the timeliness of feedback, help identify learning difficulties, and support evidence-informed educational decisions. However, these benefits are not automatic: they depend on pedagogical design, data quality, transparency, privacy safeguards, and meaningful human oversight. The article proposes a functional integration model that connects learner data, AI-based analysis, personalized recommendations, an intelligent assistant, and teacher review. Since the study is conceptual, the proposed model requires empirical evaluation before claims about its effectiveness can be made.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Optometry: Awareness and Perspectives Among Scandinavian Optometrists
items.abstract: The awareness and perspectives of Scandinavian optometrists regarding artificial intelligence (AI) in eye care was evaluated through a web-based questionnaire. Responses from 421 optometrists were analyzed for familiarity, perceived benefits, concerns, and willingness to engage with AI technologies. Most participants expressed familiarity with AI and support for its inclusion in education and practice, though concerns regarding diagnostic accuracy and potential impacts on the patient-optometrist relationship were noted. These findings are critical for informing educational strategies and facilitating knowledge exchange aimed at addressing uncertainties and optimising the benefits of AI in eye care.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Reducing the Impacts of Urban Flooding
items.abstract: This paper examines the multifaceted contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to urban flood-risk reduction, with particular emphasis on data-driven forecasting, real-time monitoring, infrastructure management, emergency response, recovery, and resilient urban planning. AI technologies—including machine learning, predictive analytics, remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) networks, natural language processing, and image analysis—can support more accurate flood prediction, dynamic risk assessment, optimized drainage operations, and timely public communication. The paper also discusses the integration of AI into smart-city frameworks, the limitations of conventional flood-management approaches, challenges associated with data quality and availability, computational requirements, ethical considerations, and the need for interdisciplinary collaboration. In addition, an embedding-based long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture is presented for probabilistic streamflow forecasting in settings in which individual weather products may be unavailable. However, effective implementation requires robust data infrastructures, transparent model-development practices, appropriate institutional capacity, and supportive policy frameworks.

items.abstract: Abstract Motivation is central to successful English language learning because it influences effort, persistence, participation, and willingness to communicate. This thesis examines how gamification can support student motivation through a literature-based analysis of recent research. It argues that selected game elements may increase engagement when they promote competence, autonomy, meaningful progress, and social interaction. However, gamification is not automatically effective. Its value depends on careful alignment with language objectives, learner needs, and balanced classroom implementation. items.title: The Smart Buildings Challenge: Learning Foundation Models for Real-World Optimization at Scale
items.abstract: Buildings cause nearly 40\% of carbon emissions in the US. Of total building emissions, HVAC systems are responsible for approximately 40-60\% and account for 15\% of global energy consumption. Despite advances in artificial intelligence, most buildings still operate as inefficiently as they did decades ago. Building optimization, perhaps more so than any other optimization problem, has enormous potential for Machine Learning (ML) driven impact on climate change, in both the short and long term. One of the biggest obstacles for building optimization is the lack of policy transfer. Most building control systems, whether simulation or learning based, don't generalize: they only work well for the building they were developed for, but not for other buildings. To solve this problem, we propose a challenge for the development of building foundation models that easily adapt to new buildings with minimal configuration and thereby enable building optimization to scale across the globe. Participants will build control policies on a set of simulated buildings, and have their policies evaluated on an unseen set of buildings. The buildings vary in size, layout, weather, material properties, and HVAC system. Successful outcomes from this initiative promise a massive leap forward in global sustainability efforts and demonstrate the great potential of ML to combat climate change.

items.title: The Synthetic Performer : Economic, Labor, Technological, Legal and Ethical Dimensions of AI-Generated Actors in the Vertical Drama Industry
items.abstract: This dissertation investigates the displacement of human actors by generative AI performers in the fastest-growing segment of the screen entertainment economy: the vertical drama, or micro-drama, industry. The study is organized around a triggering case widely reported in October 2026, in which a nineteen-year-old actress, Hannah Lowery, was reportedly recast out of an ice-skating-themed series when the production shifted entirely to AI-generated performers. Using the video report as an entry point, the dissertation triangulates its claims against primary trade reporting, including Business Insider (June 2026), trade publications such as Variety, Mashable, and The Economic Times, regulatory documents, and a broad interdisciplinary literature spanning cultural economics, labor sociology, media theory, and machine learning. Methodologically, the dissertation combines (i) documentary and content analysis of the video case and its verification status, examining each claim individually; (ii) economic analysis of production cost structures, drawing on reported estimates of US$1,000–US$3,000 per AI-generated episode compared with US$100,000–US$300,000 for equivalent productions featuring human casts; (iii) institutional analysis of the emerging regulatory landscape, including the 2023 SAG-AFTRA agreements, California Assembly Bill 2602 (AB 2602), Tennessee’s ELVIS Act, the proposed federal NO FAKES Act, the European Union’s AI Act, and China’s provisions governing deep synthesis and generative AI; and (iv) the construction of forward-looking scenarios for the coming decade. The central argument is threefold. First, vertical dramas constitute a genuine entry-level market for synthetic performance in a manner consistent with disruption theory: their economics are driven by cost minimization and production volume rather than the premium emotional differentiation characteristic of high-end productions. Second, the displacement pressure documented in 2026 is driven less by audience preferences than by production-cost arbitrage and platformization dynamics. Survey evidence indicates that Western audiences still overwhelmingly prefer human stars, whereas Chinese production has already shifted substantially toward AI-generated content. Third, the emerging legal and ethical framework—encompassing consent, compensation, disclosure, and posthumous rights—will determine whether the industry converges toward regulated coexistence or experiences a cascade of substitutions with severe consequences for the talent pipeline. The dissertation contributes a verified factual foundation, a production cost-structure model, a four-scenario matrix, and a policy agenda for performers, producers, platforms, and regulators.
